title: House Robber
problemStatement:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed, the only constraint stopping you from robbing each of them is that adjacent houses have security systems connected and it will automatically contact the police if two adjacent houses were broken into on the same night.

Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

examples.explanation: Rob house 1 (money = 1) and then rob house 3 (money = 3). Total amount you can rob = 1 + 3 = 4.
Rob house 1 (money = 2), rob house 3 (money = 9) and rob house 5 (money = 1). Total amount you can rob = 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.

solutions.description: Use pure recursion to explore all possible robbing patterns. At each house, decide whether to rob it (and skip the next house) or skip it (and consider the next house). The base case returns 0 when reaching beyond the array. This brute force approach has exponential time complexity due to overlapping subproblems.

solutions.detailedExplanation: This recursive solution directly models the robbing decision at each house. From house i, we have two choices: (1) skip this house and consider the maximum from house i+1 onward, or (2) rob this house (gaining nums[i]) and consider the maximum from house i+2 onward (since we cannot rob i+1). The base case returns 0 when we go beyond the array, meaning no more money can be collected. We recursively compute both options and return the maximum. This builds a decision tree where each path represents a valid robbing sequence. However, the tree has exponential size because we recompute the same subproblems many times. For example, computing rob(5) might involve computing rob(4) and rob(3), but rob(4) also computes rob(3), leading to redundant work.
commonMistakes: Not handling the base case correctly (infinite recursion)
Adding nums[i+1] instead of recursing to i+1 (incorrect skip logic)
Recursing to i+1 when robbing instead of i+2 (violating adjacent constraint)
Starting recursion from wrong index (should start at 0)
Forgetting to return the maximum of both choices
solutions.whyItWorks: The recursion correctly explores all valid robbing sequences by making the skip-or-rob decision at each house. The constraint that adjacent houses cannot be robbed is enforced by jumping to i+2 when we rob house i. The base case handles the termination correctly. By taking the maximum at each decision point, we bubble up the optimal solution. However, the overlapping subproblems (same houses considered multiple times through different paths) make this approach inefficient.
keyInsights: Problem has optimal substructure: optimal solution uses optimal solutions to subproblems
Two choices at each house: skip (consider i+1) or rob (take nums[i] and consider i+2)
Robbing house i forces us to skip i+1, naturally encoded by recursing to i+2
Exponential time due to overlapping subproblems being recomputed

solutions.detailedExplanation: This memoized solution adds a cache array to the recursive approach. The memo array stores the maximum money that can be robbed starting from each house i. Before computing a result, we check if it's already cached. If memo[i] != -1, we return the cached value immediately. Otherwise, we compute it recursively (max of skip or rob), store it in memo[i], and return it. This eliminates redundant computation: each house's maximum is computed exactly once, then reused whenever needed. Since there are n houses and each is computed once in O(1) time (after dependencies are resolved), the total time is O(n). The space complexity is O(n) for the memo array plus O(n) for the recursion stack depth.
commonMistakes: Using 0 as the memo sentinel value (conflicts with valid result of 0)
Not initializing memo array properly (undefined behavior)
Forgetting to store result in memo before returning (no memoization benefit)
Storing at wrong index or with wrong value (incorrect results)
Not checking memo before making recursive calls (defeating memoization)
solutions.whyItWorks: Memoization transforms the exponential recursive tree into linear computation. Each subproblem (maximum money from house i onward) is solved exactly once. The first time we reach house i, we compute and cache the result. All subsequent reaches of house i return the cached value in O(1) time. Since there are n unique subproblems and each takes O(1) time to compute after dependencies are cached, the total time is O(n). The memo array acts as a lookup table that prevents redundant recursive calls.
keyInsights: Memoization eliminates overlapping subproblem recomputation
memo[i] stores maximum money robbing from house i to end
Each subproblem solved exactly once, reducing exponential to linear
Top-down approach: start with full problem, break into subproblems as needed
Space-time trade-off: O(n) space for O(n) time

solutions.detailedExplanation: This bottom-up DP approach builds the solution iteratively from the base cases upward. We create a DP array where dp[i] represents the maximum money that can be robbed from houses 0 through i (inclusive). The base cases are: dp[0] = nums[0] (rob the first house) and dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1]) (rob whichever of the first two houses has more money). For any house i ≥ 2, we have two choices: (1) don't rob house i, giving us dp[i-1], or (2) rob house i, giving us nums[i] + dp[i-2]. We take the maximum: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2]). We fill the array left to right, and finally dp[n-1] contains the maximum money that can be robbed from all houses. This approach avoids recursion overhead and is straightforward to implement.
commonMistakes: Not handling empty array or single house cases (array access errors)
Incorrect base case for dp[1] (should be max of first two houses, not just nums[1])
Starting loop at wrong index (should start at 2, not 0 or 1)
Incorrect recurrence relation (forgetting to add nums[i] when robbing)
Off-by-one errors in array indexing
solutions.whyItWorks: The bottom-up approach works by recognizing that the maximum money from houses 0 to i depends only on the maximums from 0 to i-1 and 0 to i-2. We either don't rob house i (keeping the previous maximum dp[i-1]), or we rob house i (adding nums[i] to the maximum from two houses back, dp[i-2]). By computing in order from smallest to largest index, we ensure all dependencies are available when computing dp[i]. The recurrence correctly captures the constraint that adjacent houses cannot be robbed.
keyInsights: dp[i] represents maximum money from houses 0 through i
Base cases: dp[0] = nums[0], dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1])
Recurrence: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2])
Bottom-up approach: build from base cases to target
No recursion overhead, just a simple loop

solutions.detailedExplanation: This space-optimized solution uses the same recurrence as the bottom-up approach but recognizes that we only need the last two DP values. We maintain two variables: rob1 represents dp[i-2] (maximum money two houses back), and rob2 represents dp[i-1] (maximum money one house back). For each house, we compute the new maximum as max(num + rob1, rob2) - either rob the current house (adding to rob1) or don't rob it (keeping rob2). We store this in temp, then slide our window forward: rob1 = rob2, rob2 = temp. After processing all houses, rob2 contains the maximum money. The initialization rob1=0, rob2=0 handles the base cases implicitly: when processing the first house, rob1=0 means we're starting fresh, and rob2=0 means we haven't robbed anything yet.

Incorrect initialization (should both be 0)
Updating variables in wrong order (need temp to preserve old value)
Forgetting that rob1 represents two houses back, rob2 represents one house back
Trying to update both variables simultaneously without temp
solutions.whyItWorks: The space optimization works because the DP recurrence dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2]) only looks back two positions. By maintaining a sliding window of the last two values, we can compute each new value without storing the entire array. The variables rob1 and rob2 track dp[i-2] and dp[i-1] respectively. Computing max(num + rob1, rob2) gives us dp[i], then we slide forward by updating rob1 = rob2 and rob2 = newValue. This maintains the same correctness as the array approach but uses O(1) extra space.

rob1 tracks dp[i-2], rob2 tracks dp[i-1]

Temp variable necessary to preserve old rob2 when updating
Optimal space-time trade-off: O(n) time, O(1) space
Handles edge cases naturally through 0 initialization
